t: Count Special Quadruplets: From Four Loops to a Hash Map
o: We must count index quadruplets a < b < c < d with nums[a] + nums[b] + nums[c] = nums[d]. In [1,1,1,3,5] the four answers come from 1+1+1=3 once and 1+1+3=5 three times, which shows that equal values still produce distinct quadruplets because the indices differ. Constraints are tiny (n at most 50, values at most 100), so even examining every quadruplet is acceptable; nevertheless the structure of the equation, a pair sum on the left against a difference on the right, invites a hash-map speedup to O(n^2).
k: The ordering constraint is over indices, not values, so duplicates legitimately generate multiple quadruplets.
Rewriting nums[a] + nums[b] + nums[c] = nums[d] as nums[a] + nums[b] = nums[d] - nums[c] splits it into two independent halves.
Processing split points left to right lets a hash map hold exactly the pair sums whose both indices precede c.
With values bounded by 100, sums and differences live in a tiny range, making hash maps effectively arrays.

a.i: The definition is literally a predicate over ordered index quadruples, so enumerate a, b, c, d in nested increasing loops and count hits. With n at most 50 the work stays around six million equality checks, well within limits. This direct translation is the safest starting point in an interview.
s: Loop a from 0 to n-4, b from a+1 onward, c from b+1 onward, d from c+1 onward.
Increment the answer whenever nums[a] + nums[b] + nums[c] equals nums[d].
a.t: O(n^4) since all ordered quadruplets are enumerated, about 6 million comparisons for n = 50.

a.i: Rearrange the equation to nums[a] + nums[b] = nums[d] - nums[c]: a pair on the left, a difference on the right. Sweep c left to right while a map holds counts of sums nums[a] + nums[b] with both indices strictly left of c; for every d > c add the stored count of nums[d] - nums[c]. Only after querying do we insert all pairs ending at c, which preserves a < b < c < d exactly.
s: Initialize an empty multiset (hash map) of pair sums.
For each c in increasing order, first query: for every d > c add pair[nums[d] - nums[c]] to the answer.
Then insert: for every a < c increment pair[nums[a] + nums[c]].
The insert-after-query order guarantees both pair indices are smaller than c.
a.t: O(n^2) since each index serves once as c scanning later ds and once as the right endpoint of inserted pairs, all with O(1) map operations.
a.sp: O(D) where D is the number of distinct pair sums; with values up to 100 the sums lie in [2, 200], so this is constant in practice.

w: Start with the four-loop brute force to lock down correctness, then offer the pair-sum sweep as the optimization. Watch for: counting duplicate values correctly because indices distinguish quadruplets, keeping a < b < c < d strict by inserting pairs only after queries, and remembering differences can be negative so array-of-offsets tricks must shift indices. A natural follow-up is generalizing to k-tuples or handling negative numbers, which the hash-map version already tolerates.
